title: William Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice
full_review:
Is Shakespeare's famous character Shylock a bloodthirsty inhuman monster, or a justly vengeful Jewish victim of years of Christian abuse?

That conundrum is what's kept Shakespeare's classic play off the movie screen for decades, while stage and television productions, which have been relatively numerous, lean toward the latter interpretation. That is precisely the course taken by director Michael Radford and star Al Pacino as Shylock in this first big-screen adaptation of modern times.

"The Merchant of Venice" (Sony Pictures Classics) receives a richly visual -- if, at times, as murky as a Venetian canal -- on-location filming that is remarkably faithful to Shakespeare's story. Cuts have been made in the text, of course, but nothing damaging, and the film is absorbing, if somewhat somber and leisurely paced.

In the interest of political correctness, the film opens with a written prologue which informs us that "intolerance of the Jews was a fact of 16th-century life," and describes how they were forced to live in the ghetto and practice usury.

The time is 1596, and young Bassanio (Joseph Fiennes) confides in his friend, a wealthy merchant named Antonio (Jeremy Irons), that he is in love with a bewitching noblewoman named Portia (Lynn Collins), and asks Antonio for a loan so he can win her. The latter is currently cash-poor, but is expecting three ships carrying bountiful riches within the next couple of months.

The two men -- who, in this telling, demonstrate a closeness that may stop just short of the sexual, though there's a brief kiss between them -- turn to Shylock, the moneylender, for the needed 3,000 ducats. Shylock agrees to loan the money, with the proviso -- inserted in a "merry spirit," he assures them -- that if Antonio cannot repay the money, Shylock may exact a pound of Antonio's flesh.

Bassanio succeeds in wooing Portia over two other hopeful suitors. Likewise, her lady-in-waiting, Nerissa (Heather Goldenhersh), is courted by Bassanio's sidekick, Gratiano (Kris Marshall).

Meanwhile, Shylock's daughter, Jessica (Zuleikha Robinson), falls in love with and elopes with the Christian Lorenzo (Charlie Cox), much to her father's grief.

After the three months of his contract with Shylock, Antonio's ships are reported lost at sea, and Shylock insists on making good on his bond, extracting the "pound of flesh" which would, of course, kill Antonio.

Bassanio tells Portia, whom he's now married, the whole story of his friendship with Antonio, and the latter's sacrifice on his behalf.

The matter comes to trial, and Portia and Nerissa come to court disguised as a male barrister and his assistant, and proceed to argue for the merchant's life, offering Shylock twice the original amount of money, which he refuses. It is during this scene that Portia delivers the famous "quality of mercy" speech quoted as much as some biblical passages.

Shylock is resolute in wanting his revenge, and just when Portia seems to be relenting that Antonio has no recourse, she is able to thwart Shylock with a technicality. If, she argues, in cutting the pound of flesh, he spills one drop of "Christian blood," all his goods will be confiscated.

By the time Shylock leaves the courtroom, a broken man, he has lost nearly everything and been told he must convert to Christianity, which, in Pacino's portrayal, destroys him more than anything else.

Pacino gives a well-thought-out interpretation, with a mostly convincing Jewish cadence in his speech, just ever so slightly crossing into a New York Jewish patois, and his defeat and humiliation at the end are most pitiable. His "Hath not a Jew eyes?" speech is delivered with great conviction.

Screen newcomer Collins gives a really splendid account of Portia. Collins is the epitome of grace and loveliness in the early scenes, and then, made up as the barrister with a little moustache and goatee, she is quite effective in the courtroom scene. Her English accent is flawless, and you'd never dream she hailed from Texas.

Irons makes an excellent Antonio, and his (justifiable) fear in the courtroom, as he is forced to bear his breast before the expected cutting, is palpable. Fiennes -- back in "Shakespeare in Love" territory -- is solid as Bassanio, torn between his love for Portia and his ties to his old friend.

The homosexual subtext between Antonio and Bassanio has been done before in stage productions, as a way of explaining why Antonio would take such an extraordinary risk for his young friend (that is, putting his life on the line to get Antonio the money he needs). Actually, the film has a good payoff of this interpretation near the end, where Portia, who seems to intuit the unusually strong ties between her husband and the merchant, exacts an assurance of his love and commitment to her.

The location shooting in Venice makes for ideal authenticity, it goes without saying, though the brief shots of topless prostitutes standing on a bridge amid the teeming crowds, is rather gratuitous, however authentic it might be.

All in all, the story is well told and will appeal to lovers of theater and Shakespeare, and students of the same. A recent National Theatre production, directed by Trevor Nunn, which was filmed and shown on PBS's "Masterpiece Theatre" was, on the whole, more consistently superior, though it was a more studio-bound production. But, as a big-screen version, Radford's film is satisfying.

Due to some nudity and sexual innuendo, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
